title: Velmar
kind: Demo for a client · online store and back office
summary: An end-to-end clickable demo of the online store and back office of a Mar del Plata workshop that makes personalized goods: name collars, photo lamps, candles and NFC plaques. It has a live customizer, a coupon wheel, a club with missions, and gifting. Everything runs in the browser, on sample data.

facts.v: A real workshop in Mar del Plata
65 screens: 24 in the store, 41 in the panel
Demo: no real payments or orders

tldr.v: Every order starts in a chat, gets written into a spreadsheet and scheduled on a phone calendar. Payment receipts by chat, stock by hand, delivery dates by guesswork.
A store where buyers see their product before paying, and a panel that takes each order from the receipt to the machine to delivery.
A navigable demo on sample data, made to show before the project starts. There is no production version and no results to show.

p: Velmar is a real workshop in Mar del Plata. I built a demo of its online store and its back office, so the owners could see their business working before the project starts.
list: Store, built for phones: 17 sample products in 10 categories, a collar customizer with a live preview, photo personalization, cart, four-step checkout and order tracking.
Club: a coupon wheel, chained missions, a prize wallet, gifts with an opening scene, and 16 seasonal themes.
Panel: orders, manual payments, a production queue, a delivery calendar with daily capacity, supplies, costs and margins, simulated automatic emails, and a content studio for Instagram.
How it runs: entirely in the browser. It processes no payments, creates no real orders and calls no external services.

p: The demo script starts from a familiar scene: every order starts in a chat, gets written into a spreadsheet and scheduled on a phone calendar. That is where the pains the demo goes after come from.
list: Payment receipts arriving by chat, and updates sent to each customer one by one.
Stock and prices kept by hand in a spreadsheet.
Not knowing which delivery date to promise.
Not knowing whether each product makes money.
Not knowing what to post on Instagram.

p: What the demo proposes, not results: there are no real sales to show.

items.d: The customizer and photo personalization show the result live, with a price that changes with each option.
«When will it arrive?» counts working days without holidays and, if the first days are full, offers the first date with room in the workshop's capacity.
A coupon wheel, club missions, 16 seasonal themes with their own coupon, and reminders for the pet's birthday and for re-buying candles and scents.
A gift code and link: the recipient never sees the price and opens it with one of 17 scenes for the occasion.
The demo comes with a 10-minute meeting script («Don't sell features, sell hours») and a list of everything added beyond the spec, sized S, M or L, to decide what goes in. It is not a quote.

p: The store's incentives all end up in one place: a coupon in «My coupons». The cart validates everything with a single rule, and the panel controls every source.

diagram.title: Wheel, club and coupons
diagram.caption: Sample data. In the demo everything happens in the browser; in production, the draw, the coupons and mission progress would be computed on the server.

wheel.label: Wheel
wheel.note: A weighted draw in a pure function with injectable randomness: the animation only decides where it stops. It is offered once per browser.

wallet.label: My coupons
wallet.note: It gathers the wheel coupon, the current theme's coupons and the store's, usable ones first. Prizes are single-use and expire; other people's wheel coupons never show up.

club.label: Velmar Club
club.note: Chained missions, such as «Buy 2 products». Progress is illustrative: in production only paid orders would count.

panel.label: Panel
panel.note: Each slice with its prize and weight, and the resulting probability. A visible wheel can't be saved without a positive weight. Missions have their own simulator.

p: Order states are a state machine with rules: each change says who can make it. The panel only offers valid transitions, bulk changes included.

diagram.title: The states of an order
diagram.caption: Every change leaves an email in a simulated outbox. Not drawn: cancelling before payment, and claims and returns.

review.label: Under review
review.note: Uploading a receipt never marks the order as paid: it puts it under review. Approving asks for confirmation; rejecting requires a reason.

paid.label: Paid
paid.note: There are two ways to «Paid»: an admin approving the receipt, or the provider's confirmation. In the demo, Mercado Pago's is a button that stands in for the webhook.

prod.label: In production
prod.note: Leaving «To be made» deducts the recipe's supplies, exactly once. From finishing it can go back to the machine; a ready order never goes back to production.

ready.label: Ready
ready.note: With pickup at the workshop it goes straight to delivered; with shipping, to shipped first.

p: It is the product that best shows the idea: buyers build their collar and see the result before paying. Behind it are pure rules that the workshop, the cart and the emails all read the same way.
collar.title: From options to the workbench
collar.caption: Options the workshop hasn't confirmed yet are marked «demo example», in the order too.

steps.d: Letter style, typeface, color, cord and pattern, material, charm and neck size. The SVG preview updates live.
If the pattern uses a second color, it contrasts with the cord; an ornament that doesn't go with that letter style is dropped.
The price changes with each option, in whole pesos.
By neck size, with ranges that leave no gaps. Out of range, it offers a made-to-measure order over WhatsApp.
Adding to the cart is approving the design: the moment of approval is saved with the configuration.
A short description travels to the cart, the order, the production queue and the emails.

p: Today it is a single Next app exported to static HTML: the store and the panel share a rules engine and the data in this browser. The production plan replaces the demo panel and moves the rules to the server.

diagram.title: One static app, two faces, one engine
diagram.caption: Top: what is built, a static export on GitHub Pages with no server or database. Bottom: what the repo's documentation plans, not built.

admin.label: Demo panel
admin.note: No login on purpose: it protects nothing, says so on screen and won't be migrated. The real panel replaces it.

engine.label: Rules engine
engine.note: Prices, coupons, states, delivery dates and draws in pure functions, with amounts in whole pesos. Tested without React.

data.label: Demo data
data.note: Sample data plus the changes saved in this browser: what the panel edits shows up in the store of the same browser, and nowhere else.

server.label: Next server
server.note: Login with an admin role checked on the server, and a single transition function inside a transaction with its audit trail.

p: A demo doesn't have to protect anything, but it has to be honest about what it doesn't protect, and not leave bad habits for production.

items.t: A panel with no login, and it says so
items.d: There is no fake login: the panel says on screen that it isn't secure, and it is never reused as authorization. The real panel has a login and a role checked on the server.
States only change through valid transitions, and a receipt puts the order under review. Checkout says that nothing is charged.
Number, expiry and code are validated so the form feels real, but only the brand, the last 4 digits and the expiry are stored. In production, the workshop would never receive the number or the code.
Photos are processed in the browser and never leave it. Text takes no emoji and has a maximum length; photos are JPG, PNG or WebP up to 10 MB. In production, the same rules run again on the server.
The code has a check digit and the link is versioned: cut or edited, it opens nothing. It never carries an email or a price.
CI runs with minimal permissions and no secrets. The demo asks not to be indexed, because it shows sample prices of a real business.

items.t: A static demo today, the same app tomorrow
items.why: It had to be shown before the project started, with no infrastructure or real data: a static export, with no Server Actions, cookies or middleware. For production, the demo is frozen on its branch and main gains a server, Prisma and login; components are reused because they only take props.
Prices, coupons, states, dates and draws live in functions without React, with injectable randomness. They are tested on their own and, in production, move to the server, which recomputes everything.

items.t: Adding to the cart approves the design
items.why: That is the moment the buyer is looking at the preview. The approval is saved right there and travels with the order to the workshop.
items.alt: A separate «That's the one» checkbox, as the spec had it.

items.t: Everything beyond the spec, in writing
items.why: Every addition (the wheel, the themes, the emails, the content studio…) goes on a list with what it would need in production and an S, M or L size. That is how the client decides what goes in and at what price.

Tables have «View as spreadsheet» (keyboard, ranges, copy and paste, undo), Excel or CSV import with a per-row preview, and export. Computed values and states are read-only, and everything is saved through one path: the engine's.

Scenes, the wheel, the cart and search load when needed, and content further down isn't drawn until you get close. The repo's QA log records, on an emulated Pixel 7 with a 4× CPU, the home page's total blocking time (TBT) going from 3474 to 1727 ms. I didn't measure it again.

p: The repo's CI runs, in order: lint, type checks, unit tests, build, an export check and the e2e tests on an emulated phone. It only deploys from main.

items.d: Unit tests with Vitest, in 33 files
E2E with Playwright on an emulated Pixel 7, in 49 files

quality.note: I ran the 256 unit tests on 10/28/2026: all passed. I listed the 367 Playwright tests with --list that day and didn't run them. I counted the screens and modules in the code.

status.h: Status, and what I don't claim
list: A demo made for a client: a real workshop in Mar del Plata. It processes no payments, creates no real orders and calls no external services.
It is not in production and doesn't sell. There are no sales or repeat-purchase metrics: customers, orders, pets, costs and supplies are made up, and prices are samples.
The panel isn't secure: it has no login, on purpose.
The production pieces (server, database, login, payments with a webhook, real emails and private file storage) are planned, not built.
Pending: checking several details on a real iPhone and iPad, and the workshop confirming which collar styles it makes.
Volta, another demo in the lab, started as a copy of this repo: the panel, checkout and gifting were built here first.
